title: Mark Cuban Says Every Worker Deserves Company Stock: 'If CEOs Get 10%, Janitors Should Too'
excerpt: The billionaire entrepreneur argues that universal employee stock ownership, not tax policy, is the most effective tool to address America's widening income inequality.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Mark Cuban advocates for universal employee stock ownership to combat income inequality.
  • Cuban believes stock ownership is more effective than tax increases for wealth distribution.
  • His proposal aligns with trends in Silicon Valley and the Indian tech industry.
  • Cuban's ideas are gaining attention from business leaders and policymakers alike.

  • Mark Cuban proposes that if CEOs receive 10% of their compensation in company stock, every employee from the janitor to the C-suite should receive the same percentage — a policy he says would "change the game" on income inequality.
  • Cuban argues that raising taxes on the wealthy won't materially change the economy, but giving workers ownership stakes would create broad-based wealth building.
  • The proposal echoes employee stock ownership plans (ESOPs) that have gained traction in Silicon Valley and across the Indian tech industry, where stock-based compensation is a primary wealth driver for H-1B professionals.
  • Cuban has been increasingly vocal on economic policy, drawing attention from both business leaders and policymakers.

The Proposal

Mark Cuban, the billionaire entrepreneur and former owner of the Dallas Mavericks, has laid out what he calls the single most effective policy to address income inequality in America: give every worker company stock, proportional to the same percentage that executives receive.

"If the CEO gets 10% of their pay in stock, then the janitor should get 10% of their pay in stock," Cuban said in recent interviews covered by Fortune, Inc., and Yahoo Finance. "That will change the game."

Cuban's argument is disarmingly simple. Stock-based compensation has been the primary engine of wealth creation in corporate America for decades, but its benefits have been concentrated almost exclusively among executives and senior management. By extending the same proportional benefit to every employee, companies would create a mechanism for broad-based wealth building without requiring government redistribution.

Why Not Just Tax the Rich?

Cuban has been blunt about the limits of tax policy as a tool for addressing inequality. "Don't worry Mark, we'll eat you last," he joked about the political appetite for taxing billionaires, before making his core argument: raising his taxes wouldn't "really change how the money is distributed" across the economy. The structural problem, in his view, isn't that the wealthy pay too little — it's that most workers have no ownership stake in the companies that generate wealth.

The distinction matters. Tax revenue flows through government programs with their own overhead, targeting, and political constraints. Stock ownership, by contrast, directly ties a worker's financial outcome to the company's success, creating alignment between labor and capital that tax policy cannot replicate.

The Diaspora Connection

Cuban's proposal has particular resonance for Indian professionals in the United States, many of whom have experienced firsthand how stock-based compensation can build generational wealth. In Silicon Valley and across the tech industry, restricted stock units (RSUs) and employee stock purchase plans have been the primary wealth driver for H-1B workers at companies like Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and Meta.

The Indian IT services industry has also embraced employee stock ownership, though the practice remains more common at startups and product companies than at traditional services firms. TCS, Infosys, and Wipro offer stock options to select employees, but the coverage is far from universal. Cuban's vision of proportional stock ownership across all levels of a company would represent a significant shift in how Indian-origin workers at American companies — and potentially their counterparts at Indian firms — think about compensation.

""That will change the game."</p> <p>Cuban's argument is disarmingly simple."

The Practical Challenges

Universal stock ownership raises logistical questions that Cuban's proposal doesn't fully address. How would it work for private companies without publicly traded shares? What happens to workers at companies whose stock declines? Employee Stock Ownership Plans, or ESOPs, already exist in American corporate law, but adoption remains limited — only about 6,500 ESOPs cover roughly 14 million workers in the United States.

Still, the idea has momentum. A growing body of research suggests that companies with broad-based stock ownership report higher productivity, lower turnover, and better financial performance. Whether Cuban's vision gains policy traction or not, it frames a question that matters to every worker with a stake in the American economy.
